verdicts.correction: The subtraction must be tied to the reaping, not to the child's last sighting. The baseline drops zombies (psutil_provider.py:102-103; see G8), so a child that has exited but is not yet reaped vanishes from the snapshot one or more ticks before its parent's child time rises. 'Subtract for every seen child that ended since the last tick' then lands in the wrong interval. The clamp swallows it there, and the next tick double counts. State that a zombie stays in the snapshot until its /proc entry is gone (G8's fix is a prerequisite), and that a pending subtraction is carried to whichever process's child time rises: the last-seen parent, or the subreaper if that parent has ended. The limits sentence overlaps R15, which edits docs/10:10 and docs/17:221.

verdicts.reason: The defect is real and in the baseline today. The re-run of verify-2/reap_counters.py printed 'this process's /proc/self/io rose at reaping by write_bytes 4.0 MiB' and 'I/O a workload holding both is charged: 8.0 MiB for 4.0 MiB written', and psutil_provider.py:77-78, sampler.py:82-83 and rules.py:208-209 take and sum the plain delta. verdicts.reason: The defect is in the built baseline, not only in a design choice. rules.py:130-163 rebuilds every attribution from the current batch alone, with no state carried between batches. Inheritance needs the parent to be in by_pid (rules.py:137,144). Once the shell exits, the server's parent is missing or stale, so _direct returns None and the server falls to Unattributed (rules.py:155-157). verify-2/attribution_checks.out.txt shows both cases: '{20: agent, 22: unattributed}'. a-linux/cgroup_totals.out.txt section 4 shows the real Linux reparenting: 'its parent is now pid 1: False, named systemd'. An orphan therefore inherits whatever workload systemd --user is given, which can be a wrong workload as well as Unattributed. No document rules on this: docs/17:77,94 and docs/14:259 give only the order and the start-time check, and R09 and R15 cover other cases. 'High' fits the definition exactly: the attribution job fails under real conditions. Detached dev servers, `nohup ... &` and Windows `start` launchers whose parent exits at once are all common. It is not critical, because tagged runs are decided by group membership. raw.py:132-133,158-169 confirm the second half: the process row records the workload it had when first seen.
verdicts.correction: The proposed fix needs one more trigger. Under 'rules are retried only when exe or cmdline changes', a rules.toml reload (an epoch event, docs/17:130) would never reach live processes that inherited their workload. Add 'or when the rules file or inherit_from_parent changes'. Also add the case where an orphan is adopted by a subreaper that matches another rule (systemd --user, per cgroup_totals 4), so the test covers wrong-workload as well as unattributed.

verdicts.reason: The false statement is real. docs/17:62 says the kernel totals are authoritative for memory, and docs/05:52 and 09:9 ('Full') say the same. No gate depends on memory: the P2 gate at 17:270 and 15:17 is about CPU charge, survival, re-attach and return. No job fails either, because tagged memory is still delivered from USS. verdicts.correction: W1's text for docs/05:52 ('the kernel totals CPU and I/O') directly conflicts with L3's ('CPU and memory, and on Windows I/O and processes started'). I/O and processes started: kernel on Windows (BASIC_AND_IO_ACCOUNTING, TotalProcesses); unavailable from the kernel on Linux, with L3's decision. Memory: current memory is the sum of USS/PSS over live members on both systems. The kernel peak is kept only under its own label: peak commit on Windows, charged memory including file cache on Linux (L4).

verdicts.reason: Confirmed. docs/17:67 still offers 'a small detached holder, or the collector. Choose one and test it.' Say that the holder is the launcher's own detached part and writes the final totals by atomic rename only after the launcher's last write. Otherwise the run file has two writers (see also B7).

verdicts.reason: The mechanism is documented: nested-job accounting is aggregated in every parent (quotes in the record). The brief expects nesting, at docs/17:62 '(nested jobs)' and docs/03:53 'nested jobs available'. It still has no rule for which group a process belongs to, and no subtraction rule; I grepped docs/ for nested, innermost and parent run. Per docs/17:68, the collector reads group totals each tick, so an outer tagged run reports its inner runs' CPU as well, and cost and diff count it twice. A reasonable builder would not fix this unprompted, because docs/17:62 calls the group totals authoritative. It is plausible for this owner: a shell alias or agent workflow that wraps nested `claude`/build invocations in `submeter run` triggers it. It stays high, not critical, because a deliberate nesting of two Submeter runs is required.
verdicts.correction: The SUBMETER_RUN_ID environment variable can be lost (sudo, env -i, sandboxed agent shells), and then the double count returns silently. Say that the inner launcher confirms membership on Windows with IsProcessInJob against the outer job opened by name, and records 'parent unknown' when the variable is missing. Also align with L2's Linux layout: a nested run made as a sibling under the outer payload is included in payload's cpu.stat. So the subtraction rule must apply on Linux too, or the outer run reads payload/main only.

I re-checked this in the local systemd 255 man page (man systemd.resource-control). Under Delegate=: 'If true, delegation is turned on, and all supported controllers are enabled for the unit' and 'any controllers that are delegated will be enabled for the parent and sibling units of the unit with delegation'. Under 'Enabling and disabling controllers': 'Units for which a controller is enabled may be subject to resource control even if they don't have any explicit configuration.' The probe output (a-linux/cgroup_side_effects.out.txt) agrees: app.slice passes down cpu while a Delegate=yes scope lives, and a process's share moves from 20% to 50%. I did not re-run it, because it burns CPU and changes cgroup state. The brief sends the builder to 'cgroup v2 delegation' docs (17:42). Delegation is needed for any holder/payload layout that keeps counters after the payload empties, which is L2's own design. And Delegate=yes is the default form. So the natural build breaks fixed rule 1. Enabling cpu on 22 sibling groups changes their CPU distribution, and it exposes cpu.weight and cpu.max on them: literally 'a setting that enables' a priority change or cap (AGENTS.md rule 1). A broken fixed rule is critical by definition.
verdicts.correction: The impact line 'changes the tagged run's own CPU share, i.e. the figure being measured' describes an observer effect, not a wrong number; cpu.stat still measures what was used. The rule-1 breach alone carries critical. The man page confirms that the fix works where the parent passes nothing down: 'Assigning the empty string will enable delegation, but reset the list of controllers'. So say 'Delegate= with the parent's pass-down list, or an empty list'. On systemd 254 or later, DelegateSubgroup= can also place the payload without moving processes by hand.

verdicts.reason: Re-ran leak_checks.py: identical. My own check makes the warm-up half stronger, because it does not depend on the reviewer's sliding 2-hour window (audit_growth_windows.out.txt). With a window that grows from the start of the series, as docs/06:64 '2 to 48 h back' reads, the docs/07 warm-up is falsely flagged in 18 of 60 runs at +/-40 MB. When the warm-up is already 30 minutes old as the series begins (collector or window starting after the browser), it is falsely flagged in 22 of 60 runs at +/-20 MB with a growing window and 15 of 60 with a sliding one. Cause: growth.py:53 compares a noisy 40-point tail with 25% of the whole-window slope, so a flat tail can pass by noise. The R11 fix (docs/16:117-121, 'a leak needs sustained growth with no plateau') therefore fails under realistic per-bucket noise. A noise-free quiet fixture still passes, so the P3 gate hides it, and production raises false leak findings. That is a silent failure of the trends job: high.
verdicts.correction: The staircase sub-claim depends on the 2-hour sliding window: with a growing window it is flagged in 53 of 121 checks. It is the weaker half, and 'make the window span at least two steps' is not a usable rule because step periods have no bound. State instead that the window grows to 48 h. The suggested replacement, a tail lower confidence bound that must clear min_slope, would make true leaks hard to flag: a 75 MiB/h leak passes only 38% of the time at +/-40 MB (audit Part 4), which breaks M3's proposed acceptance. The planned task must tune M4's test and M3's acceptance rate together, for example with a longer minimum tail span or a point estimate against min_slope. verdicts.reason: Re-ran privacy_recheck.py and got identical P3 lines: 'scrub bad item is last arg: ticks UnicodeEncodeError x3; system_raw rows 0', and with exe_only a bad exe still raises UnicodeEncodeError. The code matches: one transaction per tick (raw.py:96), _register runs before self._memory is set (raw.py:132-133 against :142), so every tick retries and fails, and the gap insert (:97-101) rolls back too. One local process, on Linux any user's (L9), blinds collection for as long as it lives, with no gap recorded. All three jobs lose that period silently, which is high. It is not critical because the lost period has no rows, so coverage drops instead of showing a wrong value.
verdicts.correction: The impact is wider than the record says. My probe docs/review/probes/audit/audit_p3_state_desync.py shows that after the bad process exits, a process first seen during the failed tick has 'process rows 0, process_raw rows 1', and its CPU from that tick is lost ('0.5 s of 1.0 s read'). The reason is that _memory, _pending and _waited (raw.py:134-146) advance before the commit and are not restored on rollback. Any exception inside write(), such as a full disk or a busy database, leaves the in-memory state and the file out of step. Add to the fix: update the in-memory maps only after the transaction commits, or restore them on exception, besides sanitising text with encode('utf-8', 'backslashreplace').

new_findings.title: A session longer than raw retention cannot be summarised exactly at its end. The brief never says totals accumulate while the session runs. Raw left at the end holds 75% (48 h) or 42% (24 h floor) of a 72 h session, and its top executables cannot be rebuilt from exe_1h
new_findings.evidence: docs/06-storage.md:74 'A session or tagged run is summarised when it ends, so its cost stays exact after its raw data is gone.' docs/04-features.md:23 says the same. docs/17-build-prompt.md:127 'When a session stops or a tagged run ends, store its exact totals per workload: CPU seconds, peak and mean memory, I/O, processes started and top executables.' No document says which tier a summary is built from, that totals accumulate during the session, or how long a session may be. Retention and budget: docs/08:80 retention.raw 48h; docs/17:141 the budget deletes raw 'never going below 24 hours'; docs/08:44 'raw retention about 38 h' and :54 'about 13 h'; docs/08:74 a session may override the interval to 250ms. files.py:121-131 expires whole day files. docs/06:75 says exe_1h keeps the top ten executables per workload per hour. docs/15:17 P2 gate: 'A session's cost reads the same before and after its raw data is deleted'. The R26 fix (docs/16:215-219) assumes the session ends before its raw data expires. No summary code exists in src/ (grep 'session|summar' finds only a cli.py docstring). Probe session_retention.out.txt, 72 h session at a steady 2.0 cores: 'retention 48h (default): expired_raw at session end -> ['2026-11-16.db'] ... raw still on disk covers 2026-11-17 00:00:00 to 2026-11-19 06:20:30: 54.3 of 72.0 h'; 'retention 24h (budget floor) ... 30.3 of 72.0 h'; 'truth: 518,400 CPU-s'; 'raw at end, retention 48h (default) 391,260 CPU-s (75.5% of truth)'; 'raw at end, retention 24h (budget floor) 218,460 CPU-s (42.1% of truth)'; 'minute buckets 518,460 CPU-s if the edge bucket is kept, 518,340 if dropped'; 'hourly buckets (minute tier cut, R147) 520,860 ... kept, 513,660 if dropped (start edge 1230 s into its bucket)'. Constructed top-executable case: 'true session top: steady with 28,800 CPU-s'; ''steady' appears in 0 of 72 hourly top-ten lists'; 'top from the exe_1h lists: burst01 with 21,600 CPU-s'.
new_findings.impact: This breaks job 1 for any session longer than raw retention. That is 48-72 h at the defaults, 24-48 h while the disk budget trims raw, and less with a 250 ms session override. The brief's wording invites a summariser that reads raw at the end. Such a summariser stores 75% or 42% of the session's CPU and I/O as 'exact' for good, and cost and diff read only that row. Sums, process starts, and peak and mean memory can be rebuilt from minute buckets to within the start-edge minute, but nothing tells the builder to do so. If R147 cuts the minute tier, the edge grows to as much as an hour (-0.9% to +0.5% here). Per-session top executables cannot be rebuilt from hourly top-ten lists at all: an executable outside one hour's top ten loses that hour. An unended session closed days later (R119) hits the same problem. The P2 gate cannot catch it, because its session ends before any raw data is deleted.
new_findings.proposed_change: docs/06-storage.md:74 and docs/17-build-prompt.md:127: 'A session's and a tagged run's totals accumulate while it runs. As each raw tick is written, or each minute bucket becomes final, the server updates an open session_summary row in history.db: it adds each workload's CPU, I/O and process starts, updates peak and time-weighted mean memory, and adds per-executable CPU and peak memory. At the end it closes the row. Nothing is recomputed from raw at the end, so a session of any length stays exact.' The open row records the last tick it includes, so that after a restart the server catches up from raw that is still on disk (bounded by R93's record of what has been rolled up). For tagged runs, CPU, I/O and process counts still come from the kernel at the end, and mean memory and top executables accumulate the same way. docs/15:17 and docs/17:270, P2 gate: add 'including a session longer than raw retention (injected clock, retention.raw of a few minutes)'.
new_findings.cost: Documents: two sentences, plus one gate clause in each of docs/15 and docs/17. Build: an accumulator in the rollup or history task, about 40 lines and 2 tests, scheduled as plan.
new_findings.verification: Searched docs/ for how a summary is built (grep 'summar', 'session_summary', 'exact totals'). The only hits are docs/04:23, 05:77, 06:74, 16:219 and 17:127, and none gives a source tier, accumulation or a length limit. Ran the baseline's own FileMap.expired_raw on placeholder day files; the CPU figures are arithmetic on the stated design. Refutation attempts: (1) Minute buckets keep exact sums, so CPU and I/O can be rebuilt to within the edge minute. That holds, so the verdict is 'with changes' and the severity medium rather than critical. (2) Sessions longer than 48 h may be rare. But the 24 h budget floor, a 250 ms override and unended sessions all shorten the threshold, and no document limits session length. (3) The top-ten case is constructed. Still, any executable outside an hour's top ten loses that hour, so the lists cannot give exact session totals in general. R26, R93, R117, R119, R147 and the H-scope nothing_found line 'Sessions: kept' were all checked, and none states the long-session case.

new_findings.title: choose_tier takes raw coverage from retention.raw, not from the files on disk. While the disk budget trims raw toward its 24 h floor, a short window 24-48 h back is sent to a raw file that has already been deleted
new_findings.evidence: query.py:40-41: 'if age <= raw_retention_s: tiers, reason = [Tier.RAW, Tier.MINUTE, Tier.HOUR], "window is inside raw retention"'. Nothing checks the store. docs/06:72 'answered from the finest tier that covers its whole window'; docs/14:332 'whose retention still covers the start of the window'. docs/17:141 'delete the oldest raw file first, never going below 24 hours'; docs/08:44 'raw retention about 38 h'. files.py:121-131 expires whole day files. Probe part 5: '20-minute window starting 2026-11-17 20:00:00 (40 h back), retention.raw 48h'; 'choose_tier -> tier=raw step=1s'; 'reason: 'window is inside raw retention''; 'files the budget may delete at its 24 h floor: ['2026-11-17.db']'; 'the window lies in 2026-11-17.db; deleted under the floor: True'.

It gets no rows, labelled raw at 1 s, although the minute file still holds that window. Longer windows go to the minute tier through the point budget and are not affected. That is the oldest raw day file left and its first tick, and the oldest minute file, or a 'covered from' value per tier that retention, the budget and roll-up keep current. Pass it in, and fold this into R100's fix. docs/14:332: 'whose data on disk still covers the start of the window'. lens_gaps: A, docs/09:15 and docs/10:53: the Windows claim that temperatures have no dependable source without administrator rights is not addressed by any finding, nothing_found line or not_checked item. The 'temperatur' search hits only A-linux, H-scope and R150. R150 treats temperatures only as a scope question (defer). Throttling detected from frequency is addressed by the A-windows not_checked item on Processor Information counters.

A, docs/09:11-12 (the Windows 'Own user only' rows for memory and disk I/O): the A-windows nothing_found line says psutil's memory_info (private) and io_counters fall back to the whole-system query for processes it cannot open. That means private bytes and I/O of other users' processes are readable on Windows, but nobody says the docs/09 rows are therefore wrong for Windows. docs/09:12 itself notes that Windows process I/O counters include non-file I/O, and GetProcessIoCounters covers 'all I/O operations performed by the specified process'. Nobody follows that through to the 'Disk bytes read and written' catalogue metric (docs/06) or the I/O verdict. Windows USS (how it is read, its cost, for which processes) is not addressed either.

A, the named area 'what performance counters return without elevation' (docs/09:17, :20): not_checked names only GPU Engine, GPU Process Memory, Processor Information and Processor Queue Length. Two other Windows readings are in no item: the counters the memory and I/O verdicts need (commit, page writes, PhysicalDisk queue and latency), and the battery reading behind on_battery_multiplier.

A, the named area 'what security software or policy on a work computer blocks': Defender ASR is covered (R129 and a not_checked item), but application-control policy is in no item. That means AppLocker, App Control for Business (WDAC) and Smart App Control. On managed machines these commonly block executables in user-writable folders, which is where uv-managed Python (%APPDATA%\uv\python), .venv\Scripts\python.exe and the submeter.exe console script live. So policy decides whether the collector or the logon task can run at all. How to check: Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective -Xml; Get-CimInstance -Namespace root\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard -ClassName Win32_DeviceGuard (CodeIntegrityPolicyEnforcementStatus, UsermodeCodeIntegrityPolicyEnforcementStatus); then run .venv\Scripts\submeter.exe doctor as a standard user.

A, windows-priorities.md item 1 (the baseline checks run on Windows): no not_checked item lists the five checks on Windows or the item's named risks, which are a test's temporary folder that cannot be removed while a database file is open, and path comparisons that assume forward slashes. Only R79 names one Windows test failure (the locked byte read through a second handle). E-baseline's Windows item points only to platform_check.py, and the pytest items in not_checked concern Python 3.12/3.13, not Windows.

A, windows-priorities.md item 8 (a swarm on Windows): three points are in no item: line endings under the LF pin in .gitattributes, a virtual environment that a running process holds open, and the absence of sandboxing on native Windows. G's nothing_found covers only path length and parallel pytest temp folders. These matter mainly at stage 3, but lens A was told to work through the file in its order.

G, the named area 'phases that are too large': no finding or nothing_found line rules on phase size. G's measurements count components per phase (P0 3, P1 9, P2 4, P3 3, P4 3, P5 1, P6 2, P7 0), and R143's impact says 'P1 is the largest phase'. No item says whether P1 fits one gate or should be split. R144 and R147 shrink it only indirectly.

H, the execution prompt lists 'the baseline code' as open to challenge: no H finding or nothing_found line says whether the build should extend the baseline (docs/14:78) or replace parts of it, given R114 (the tests catch 1 of 29 deliberately broken behaviours) and R116 (the models cannot express most of the catalogue). R116's single restructuring task is the nearest item. The other open choices the prompt names are addressed: equal weight of the jobs (R148), service, dashboard and CLI (R152 and the H nothing_found line), extra telemetry (R150), Python (H nothing_found), phase order (R143, R155), and the 25 components (R155).

Not checked contradicts R68 and R138: the A-windows item 'Monotonic clock across suspend on Python 3.13+' and the C-storage item 'Whether time.monotonic counts suspended time on Windows' both tell the owner to run `submeter top --seconds 60` across a one-minute sleep. R68 and R138 show that this check cannot fail, because any interval over 30 s is a gap and prints zero CPU. These items should use an interval under 30 s across the sleep and read the gap flag, as R138 proposes.

Not checked has stale items: E-baseline 'Plateau test on a staircase leak (lead 10)... Not reached' is verified in R57, and E-baseline 'Redaction gaps in privacy/redact.py... lead 5 covers it' is verified in R61. Both should be removed from Not checked or point to those findings.
